Islamic Revolution. In nineteen seventy-eight to nineteen seventy-nine, Iran experienced a popular uprising that overthrew the autocratic Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and established an Islamic theocracy led by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. The revolution transformed Iran into an ideologically revolutionary state, altered the geopolitics of the Middle East, and inspired Islamic movements across the Muslim world, marking a seismic shift away from secular nationalism toward religious governance.

The Shah's regime, installed after a CIA-backed coup in nineteen fifty-three, pursued rapid modernization and Western alignment while suppressing political opposition. This fostered resentment among religious scholars, bazaar merchants, workers, and intellectuals alienated by his authoritarianism. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, an exiled Shiite cleric, emerged as the revolution's spiritual leader with his doctrine of velayat-e faqih, the guardianship of the jurist, proposing that religious scholars should hold ultimate political authority rather than secular rulers.

Mass protests erupted in nineteen seventy-eight, paralyzing the economy. Strikes by oil workers, bazaaris, and public-sector employees crippled the regime. By January nineteen seventy-nine, the Shah fled and Khomeini returned to Iran to a hero's reception. Khomeini consolidated power by neutralizing secular nationalists, liberals, and communist factions within the revolutionary coalition. The hostage crisis from November nineteen seventy-nine to January nineteen eighty-one, when militants took fifty-two American hostages, rallied Iranians and isolated the new regime internationally.

The revolution institutionalized Islamic law, banned Western cultural products, required strict Islamic dress codes, and subordinated state power to a Supreme Leader answerable to religious councils, establishing the world's first modern theocracy. It triggered the Iran-Iraq War from nineteen eighty to nineteen eighty-eight, as Iraq's Saddam Hussein attacked the unstable new regime. The revolution also inspired Shiite uprisings across the region and transformed Iran into an anti-American, anti-Israeli regional power that would fundamentally reshape Middle Eastern geopolitics.
